newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- Scales seen tilted toward May FOMC hike.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- Scales seen tilted toward May FOMC hike.

text.p: Wall Street generally expects the Federal Reserve will raise short-term interest rates at its next monetary policy meeting, according to a Reuters poll.
Twenty-two of 29 economists polled said they see the Fed lifting the federal funds rate at least 25 basis points at the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on May 20.
In addition, 25 of 27 pundits predicted the central bank would have raised that target rate to at least 5.75 percent by early July from its current 5.50 percent level.
The data-starved financial markets had feasted on a hearty plate of top-tier economic data this past week and offered the markets some insight to the Fed's next possible move.
Friday's employment report caused the greatest stir.
The Labor Department reported U.S. non-farm payroll growth slowed in April to 142,000, but the unemployment rate fell to 4.9 percent, its lowest level in over 23 years.
"A 4.9-percent unemployment rate is much too tight for the Fed," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc, who expects a 25-basis point rate hike at the May meeting.
The report may "shock" the Fed, he said, adding that the central bank had been concerned when the unemployment rate hit 5.2 percent.
Michael Strauss, senior vice president and chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA), said if the Fed holds rates steady in May, a rate hike at the July meeting would be probable.
"The fact that we had one month of a dip in average hourly earnings is nothing. Chances are what we're going to see in earnings is an above-trend gain in May and June," he said.
Furthermore, Strauss noted the jobless rate is "on a trajectory" that could result in economic problems next year if it is not addressed.
Those experts in the May-move camp contend that economic growth is accelerating too fast and Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan should tap on the brakes soon.

The Commerce Department released on Wednesday the advance report on first-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which grew by a staggering 5.6 percent, the largest increase in nine years. Wall Street experts had forecast GDP to show a 4.1 percent rise.
Despite the robust unemployment rate, other data this past week showed moderate pressure on compensation inflation.
Earlier in the week, the Labor Department reported that Employment Cost Index (ECI) rose 0.6 percent in March, much lower than the consensus forecast of a 0.9 percent rise.
Benefits costs rose a meager 0.1 percent while the wages and salaries component was more in line, up 0.9 percent.
Charles Lieberman, managing director and director of financial markets research at Chase, said the Fed will not move in May because the labor cost side of the equation looks very good.

"The labor market is tight -- that's beyond dispute. But the tightness in the labor market has not yet propelled any upward movement in costs and labor costs as most clearly reflected in the ECI," Lieberman said.
"So that suggests to me that the Fed is going to feel no sense of urgency to move policy," he added.
Barclay's Iggo said the ECI report is important but the Fed will continue to act preemptively.
"They are worried about inflation picking up going forward and not in the past. That's why they will raise rates (in May)," Iggo said.
